title: A World for Gazebo: The Same Scenario File Made Into an SDF World, With the Ground, the Walls, the Posts, the Goals and the Robot Where They Belong

questions.question: Why make the Gazebo world from the scenario file?
options: The scenario format is simpler than SDF
Gazebo runs faster on generated worlds
Two copies of a wall will disagree, and the simulators then disagree about something never in dispute
So that Gazebo's physics can be switched off
questions.explanation: If each simulator had its own copy of the yard, a wall moved in one would be a difference between the simulators that has nothing to do with either.

questions.question: A wall from (0,0) to (3,4) became a box of length:
options: 3.000 m, along x
5.000 m, turned 0.927295 rad
4.000 m, along y
5.000 m, laid along x
questions.explanation: The box is as long as the segment and turned to its direction: the root of 3 squared plus 4 squared, at atan2(4, 3).

questions.question: A grade of 0.1 rising along +x is a pitch of:
options: -0.1 rad exactly
-5.7 rad
questions.explanation: A positive rotation about y tips the x axis down, so a rise along +x needs a negative pitch of the arctangent of the grade.

questions.question: Why is a goal a marker with no collision?
options: It is a place, not a thing, and a robot must be able to drive onto it
A marker with collision would be too heavy
Gazebo cannot make a ring collide
So that the lidar ignores it
questions.explanation: The goal marks where the robot should end up. If it could be bumped into, the robot could never stand on it.

questions.question: Why are faults not in the world?
options: They are in it, as plugins
Gazebo cannot simulate a GNSS outage
They would slow the physics
They concern what the sensors report, so they belong between the world and the program
questions.explanation: A GNSS outage or a lost beam is something the robot's sensors report. The adapter between the world and the program applies them.

questions.question: What hides the mistake of laying every wall along x?
options: A world with no walls
Walls longer than the ground slab
Walls written from the other end
Axis aligned walls, which are the common ones
questions.explanation: A box laid along x is right for every wall that already runs along x. A test needs a wall at an angle to show the mistake.
